dl-lal-mandir.name: Shri Digambar Jain Lal Mandir (Red Temple, Chandni Chowk)
dl-lal-mandir.hindi_name: श्री दिगंबर जैन लाल मंदिर (चाँदनी चौक, लाल किला)
dl-lal-mandir.address: Shri Digambar Jain Lal Mandir (Red Temple, Chandni Chowk), Old Delhi (Shahjahanabad), District Central Delhi, Delhi - 470001
dl-lal-mandir.description: Shri Digambar Jain Lal Mandir (Red Temple, Chandni Chowk) is an auspicious Digambar Jain pilgrimage destination situated in Old Delhi (Shahjahanabad), Delhi. The oldest and best-known Digambar Jain temple in Delhi, situated directly opposite the Red Fort at the entrance to Netaji Subhash Marg and Chandni Chowk. Established in 1656 CE during the reign of Mughal Emperor Shah Jahan, it originated as the 'Urdu Mandir' (Camp Temple) for Jain military officers and imperial merchants. Built in striking red sandstone, the complex houses ancient Jinabimbas dating from the 10th–15th centuries and the renowned Charity Birds Hospital (Jain Chidiya Aspatal) established in 1956.
dl-lal-mandir.history: When Emperor Shah Jahan shifted the Mughal capital from Agra to Shahjahanabad (Delhi) in 1648, a contingent of Jain cavalry officers and royal treasurers was granted land to establish their camp opposite the imperial citadel. In 1656, an imperial officer installed a sacred image of Lord Parshvanatha in a tent sanctuary, which gradually expanded into a permanent red sandstone structure known as the Urdu Mandir. During the later Mughal period, sacred metal and stone Tirthankara idols from ancient temples in Mewar and Gwalior were brought here for preservation. In 1800–1807, Raja Harsukh Rai and community leaders renovated the sanctum, and in the early 20th century, the imposing red sandstone shikhara was added. Carr Stephen (1876) notes the prominent commercial and spiritual status of the Digambar merchant community surrounding Chandni Chowk.
dl-lal-mandir.religious_significance: Premier spiritual and institutional landmark of the Digambar Jain community in northern India, receiving hundreds of thousands of pilgrims annually.
dl-lal-mandir.moolnayak_details: Bhagwan Rishabhanatha (Adinath), in contemplative Padmasana (Seated) posture, measuring approximately 3 feet, sculpted from Black Kasauti Stone, dating to the Medieval (c. 11th–12th Century CE), (Ancient seated Vitaraga idol with bull lanchhana, accompanied by historical brass idols of Parshvanatha and Chandraprabhu.).

dl-naya-mandir.name: Shri Digambar Jain Naya Mandir (Dharampura, Chandni Chowk)
dl-naya-mandir.hindi_name: श्री दिगंबर जैन नया मंदिर (धर्मपुरा, चाँदनी चौक)
dl-naya-mandir.address: Shri Digambar Jain Naya Mandir (Dharampura, Chandni Chowk), Old Delhi (Dharampura), District Central Delhi, Delhi - 454001
dl-naya-mandir.description: Shri Digambar Jain Naya Mandir (Dharampura, Chandni Chowk) is an auspicious Digambar Jain pilgrimage destination situated in Old Delhi (Dharampura), Delhi. A monumental Digambar Jain temple in Dharampura, Old Delhi, constructed in 1807 CE (VS 1864) by Raja Harsukh Rai, royal treasurer to Mughal Emperor Akbar II. Revered as the first Jain temple in the Mughal imperial capital to be granted an official imperial firman permitting the erection of stone shikharas (spires), which had been prohibited in Delhi for centuries. The temple houses an extraordinary subterranean Jnana Bhandar preserving priceless medieval Digambar manuscripts.
dl-naya-mandir.history: Raja Harsukh Rai, an influential Agarwala Digambar Jain merchant and imperial treasurer, secured a special royal decree (firman) from Mughal Emperor Akbar II allowing the construction of soaring stone shikharas in the walled city of Shahjahanabad. The grand consecration ceremony (Panchakalyanaka Pratishtha) in 1807 was celebrated with unprecedented splendor, attended by Digambar sanghas from across northern and western India. Raja Harsukh Rai also established a subterranean Jnana Bhandar (scriptural repository) to safeguard rare palm-leaf and handmade paper manuscripts, including illuminated texts of the Samayasara and Uttarapurana with gold calligraphy.
dl-naya-mandir.religious_significance: Renowned for its architectural magnificence, imperial historical significance, and one of northern India's richest private collections of Digambar Jain manuscripts (Jnana Bhandar).
dl-naya-mandir.moolnayak_details: Bhagwan Parshvanatha, in contemplative Padmasana (Seated) posture, measuring approximately 3.5 feet, sculpted from White Makrana Marble, dating to the 1807 CE (Constituted with ancient Pratimas), (Exquisitely polished marble image with seven-hooded serpent canopy (Dharanendra nagafana) and attendant Yaksha-Yakshi carvings.).

darshan_timings.notes: Temple opens early for morning pakhsal; visitors are requested to wear traditional clean clothes.
